original_question: A sequence (x_n) is called a minimal representation of a Cantorval or a multi-interval set if removing any infinite subsequence changes the topological type of the achievement set. For an achievable Cantorval E, is it true that (x_n) is a minimal representation for E exactly when x_n < r_{n+1} for only finitely many n, as is already known for achievable multi-interval sets?
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s exact target. It correctly identifies the notion of minimal representation, the comparison with the already-settled multi-interval case, and the precise eventual tail-inequality x_n < r_{n+1} only finitely often as the candidate characterization to extend from achievable multi-interval sets to achievable Cantorvals.
missing_details: The paper states the problem in achievement-set notation E(x_n); to make the question stand-alone, one should define E(x_n) = {Σ_{n=1}^∞ ε_n x_n : ε_n ∈ {0,1}}.
The remainder sequence must be defined explicitly: r_n = Σ_{k>n} x_k, so the condition is x_n < r_{n+1} for only finitely many n.

Because the criterion x_n versus r_{n+1} depends on the order of the terms, the representing sequence should be stated in the standard convention used in the cited source: a positive absolutely summable sequence arranged in nonincreasing order.

The phrase “minimal representation” should be stated exactly in the Cantorval case: if E(x_n) is a Cantorval, then after deleting any infinite subsequence, the achievement set of the remaining terms is not a Cantorval; for multi-interval sets, “not a multi-interval set” means “not a finite union of closed intervals.”
If the set E is named separately, the question should say explicitly that E = E(x_n) is an achievable Cantorval.
A fully paper-faithful stand-alone formulation should note that finite deletions are irrelevant to topological type, which is why minimality is phrased in terms of removing infinite subsequences.
refined_question: Let (x_n)_{n≥1} be a nonincreasing positive absolutely summable sequence, let E(x_n) = {Σ_{n=1}^∞ ε_n x_n : ε_n ∈ {0,1}} be its achievement set, and write r_n = Σ_{k>n} x_k. Assume that E(x_n) is a Cantorval, i.e. an achievable Cantorval. Recall that (x_n) is called a minimal representation of E(x_n) if, after deleting any infinite subsequence of (x_n), the achievement set of the remaining terms is no longer a Cantorval. It is known that for achievable multi-interval sets this minimality is equivalent to x_n < r_{n+1} for only finitely many n. Does the same equivalence hold for achievable Cantorvals?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently: if E(x_n) is a Cantorval, is (x_n) a minimal representation exactly when x_n ≥ r_{n+1} for all but finitely many n?
justification: This is exactly Problem 32 in Section 6 of the survey. The sentence immediately preceding it supplies the survey’s definition of minimal representation, and Problem 32 asks whether the multi-interval characterization from [23, Theorem 7.8] extends to Cantorvals. Your draft matches that target closely, but it omits the definitions of E(x_n) and r_n and does not state the standard positivity/nonincreasing convention under which the cited interval-case theorem is formulated. In the underlying source [23], Definition 7.2 gives the formal notion of minimal representation, Theorem 7.8 proves the multi-interval criterion, Corollary 7.10 restates it as the eventual inequality x_k ≥ r_{k+1}, and Proposition 3.1 explains why finite modifications do not change whether the achievement set is a Cantor set, Cantorval, or finite union of closed intervals.
